Text: Draws deep ore from Deep Ore Sources in its district until they run out. Uses up metal blocks as drill bits; stops without them. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
The first machine to bore into the deep sector. It will not be the last.
Mines deep ore without end. Build it over a Deep Ore Vein. Uses up steel as drill bits and concrete as shaft lining; stops without them. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
The vein is endless; the power bill is not.
Refines deep ore into deep iron, coal, crude oil and uranium ore. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
The ore is useless until the surface factory learns how to tame it.
A finite deposit of deep ore. Deep Drills in the same district draw from it until it is empty.
Once it is dug out, it is gone.
An endless vein of deep ore. Build a Deep Mine over it.
It never runs out. Reaching it is the hard part.
Makes fertilizer from logs and algae for the Greenhouse. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Logs and algae go in. Nobody asks about the smell.
Breeds juvenile fish from fresh fish. Build it over a river: its pens need clean water and stop if they dry out or turn to badwater. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Thousands of tiny fish and one very patient beaver.
Raises juvenile fish into fresh fish, or presses fresh fish into fish oil. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
Grow them big, then press the rest for oil.
Cans fresh fish with fish oil in metal tins. Canned fish feeds beavers and stocks the Grocery Store. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Fish in a tin: the frontier lunch, whether it likes it or not.
Makes medicine from mushrooms and algae for the Hospital and the Technical School. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Mushrooms, algae and a great deal of careful stirring.
A neighborhood shop for canned fish, rations and fermented food. Staffed and stocked with three or more foods, it gives nearby beavers up to +2 wellbeing.
Everything a busy beaver needs, two paws from home.
Serves food at its tables and makes sweet berry cake and fermented food. A meal of fresh fish, berries, fermented mushrooms and an eggplant ration gives Fine dining. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
A good meal deserves a table, a view and good company.
Treats injuries, chipped teeth, badwater contamination and radiation sickness day and night. Staffed and supplied, it gives nearby beavers up to +2 wellbeing. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Rest, clean water and a very strict ward nurse.
Grows eggplants, kohlrabi and coffee beans indoors with fertilizer. Aquaponics also raises fresh fish from juvenile fish. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Summer all year round, under glass.
Makes chemicals and polymer from crude oil and extract, and cryocoolant from polymer and grease. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
Oil and extract go in, chemistry comes out, and the smell stays.
Builds machine cores, electronics, power modules, bot parts and reinforced bot frames. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Measure twice, file once, and never sneeze near the electronics.
Filters water into pure water, leaving concentrated waste, and makes filter media and reactor coolant water. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
Every barrel tested, every filter changed on time.
Beavers study here in their free time to become metallurgists, reactor operators or flight engineers. Each school teaches one, chosen in its panel.
Night classes for beavers who want a dangerous job done properly.
Turns uranium ore into enriched fuel and reactor power cells, and reprocesses spent fuel. Its fuel leaves radioactive waste. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Yellowcake is not for eating, however much it looks like it.
Turns radioactive waste into radioactive water, cleans contaminated water and filters badwater. Haul its output away: full tanks leak. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
It turns a problem you store into a problem you can ship.
Splits pure water into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
Water goes in. Two very excitable gases come out.
Chills hydrogen and oxygen gas with cryocoolant into liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the rocket fuel. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
So cold that the frost has frost.
Builds rocket airframes and propulsion packages for the Launch Pad.
The tallest thing the colony has ever built, one piece at a time.
Turns recovered artifacts into guidance computers, mission payloads and telemetry. Staffed and powered, it lowers the launch risk. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Old human drives, new beaver math and a lot of coffee.
Launches the colony's rockets, staffed by trained flight engineers. Pick a mission as its recipe; each launch uses up the rocket and its fuel, and can fail. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Everything the colony has learned, pointed at the sky.
Makes steel and alloy from deep iron, coal and limestone. Only trained metallurgists can work here, and the work is dangerous.
Every reactor, rocket and machine core starts as a white-hot pour on this floor.
Digs up recovered artifacts anywhere with explosives. Within 10 tiles of a Human Record Cache, it also surveys the cache for 12 more.
The humans buried their warnings in the strata. Dig carefully.
Stores one fuel: liquid hydrogen or liquid oxygen. It takes fuel only while powered; without power the fuel starts to vent. Pipes: connect directly, no valve.
The coldest place in the colony, kept that way at great expense.
Employs a fisher who catches fresh fish from the shore, where clean water at least 0.5 m deep lies no more than 1.25 m below the bank.
A quiet bank, a long wait and a longer story about the one that got away.
Stores up to 5 goods, each in its own slot with its own warehouse settings. Each attached Warehouse Module adds a slot and storage.
One door, one ledger and a beaver who knows where everything is.
Adds storage and a slot to a Modular Warehouse when built beside it, on top of it, or on another attached module.
Another floor of crates, and the ledger grows a page.
Not attached to a Modular Warehouse
Cleans smog out of the air around it while powered. No workers.
What goes up the smokestack comes down in the scrubber.
Steam baths that count as a Mud Bath and a Massager and give Wet fur, all in one visit. Uses water. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
The boilers run hot so the colony can run warm.
A square where beavers dance and gather: it counts as a Dance Pit and a Campfire. Needs no power or supplies.
Every frontier town needs one place where nothing is being built.
A viewing tower: the climb counts as an Exercise Plaza and the deck as a Rooftop Terrace.
From up here, the whole frontier fits in one look.

Huge power from enriched fuel, run by trained reactor operators. It melts down if its coolant water runs out or its waste is not hauled away; pausing it is safe. Pipes: valves set to Fill and Extract.
The frontier makes power and consequences at the same scale.
Stores radioactive waste. Keep it below full: a full vault leaks radioactive water and irradiates the ground around it.
Labeled, logged and never, ever full.
Burns coal and water for power day and night. No workers. Pipes: valve set to Fill.
Black smoke, white steam and the hum of every machine in the district.

Text: First launch: lofts a telescope and archive receiver to read what the old orbital records saw.

The observatory is in orbit. Its first passes recover fragments of the old orbital records: survey images of this valley before the drought, and a faint green trail of badwater running back to a single source far upriver. The archive now knows where to look.
Debris rained over the flame trench; the observatory was lost with its rocket and fuel.
Second launch: sends a probe to a derelict orbital station to bring back its data core.

The probe docked with a silent human station and returned its data core. Among the corrupted files are intact fabrication notes and a map of the treatment works that once held the badwater back. The industrial frontier has its next design.
The probe never reached the station; the rocket broke up on ascent.
Final launch: places a long-lived beacon carrying the colony's archive and a standing signal.

The beacon is aloft and transmitting. It carries the colony's archive, the record of the badwater source and a simple message: beavers live here, and the land is healing. Whoever listens next will know the way.
The beacon was lost on ascent. The archive is safe on the ground; the colony must build and fuel another rocket.

Study the badwater: finish a Public Health Lab, a Water Treatment Plant, a Deep Drill or a Chemical Works.
Public Health Lab (Wellbeing, 1,000 science), Deep Drill (Metal, 1,000), Water Treatment Plant (Water, 1,800) or Chemical Works (Metal, 9,000). Any one will do.
Every beaver knows badwater: green, sour, and best admired from a distance. The old stories call it a sickness of the land.

The colony is no longer sure the old stories are right. Badwater behaves the same everywhere, in every spring and every badtide, as if it were made to a recipe. Somebody, it seems, wrote that recipe down.
The health lab's first badwater samples were meant to help the sick. The chemists came back with puzzled faces and a very long list of things that should not be in a river.
The treatment plant's first filter cakes came out of the press the wrong color. The exact same wrong color, every single time.
The drill crew brought up a core with something round and hollow inside it: a pipe, far older than the colony and far too big for beavers.
The chemists who turn badwater into feedstock noticed that it splits the same way, batch after batch, like a recipe someone followed carefully.
Reach the deep sector: refine 20 deep iron at a Deep Ore Processor.
The Deep Drill brings up deep ore from a Deep Ore Source; the Deep Ore Processor turns deep ore into deep iron, coal, crude oil and uranium ore.
The deep sector is not empty. Below the old riverbed run tunnels lined with enormous pipes, all of them stamped with the same three letters, VWA, and all of them heading upriver.
Painted on one pipe, with increasing underlining: NOT FOR DRINKING. Someone long ago took that very seriously.
Trace what the water carries: make 80 pure water and 10 chemicals.

Water Treatment Plants make pure water from water and filter media. Chemical Works make chemicals from crude oil and extract (the Centrifuge distills extract from badwater), or from the treatment plant's concentrated waste.

Side by side, the filter residue and the chemical feedstock tell the same story. Badwater is a mixture: fine grit from deep rock, a stubborn green dye and a dozen compounds nothing in nature bothers to make.
It is not a disease. It is runoff. Somewhere upriver, something is still leaking what the old deep pipes once carried, and the colony is going to find out what.
Open the human ruins: recover 6 artifacts at an Archive Excavation.
The Archive Excavation (Science menu, 25,000 science) opens human ruins with explosives and treated planks. An excavation within 10 tiles of a Human Record Cache also surveys it for extra artifacts.
The first finds are small and baffling: a hard hat big enough to bathe a kit in, a mug reading WORLD'S OKAYEST ENGINEER, and a sign that says HOLDING STATION 3 - AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.

Underneath, in smaller letters: UNAUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ALSO ONLY. The humans, it turns out, had a sense of humor. They also had sealed data drives, which the excavation crews are now carefully drying out.
Wake the archive: recover 20 artifacts in total.
Every artifact the Archive Excavation brings up carries a sealed human data drive. Human Record Caches surveyed by an excavation count too.

The first restored drive belongs to the Valley Water Authority. Its records describe the Deepworks, the humans' great wells and drills, which pulled ancient water and ore up from under this valley for their factories.

What the factories could not use went upriver into the Holding: a chain of sealed basins kept clean by a treatment works that ran day and night. Projected containment life: indefinite, subject to maintenance.
A memo is attached. Re: containment maintenance. Postponed to next quarter. Previous note: postponed to next quarter.
Read the last shift's records: recover 40 artifacts in total and finish a Mission Control.
Mission Control unlocks at 75,000 science. It reads the artifacts' drives into guidance computers and telemetry, so keep them coming.

The newest drives are the saddest and the tidiest. The rains failed, then the wells, then the harvests. The humans decided to leave the valley for now and follow the rain north. Nobody wrote down when now would end.

The last shift did its best. It set the treatment works to automatic, put the Holding's flush valves on a schedule to run until further notice, and switched off the lights. No further notice was ever given.
Mission Control has found one more thing: an old orbital frequency. Something up there is still answering.
Launch the Orbital Observatory from a Launch Pad.

A launch needs rocket airframes, propulsion packages, guidance computers, recovered telemetry, liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, and flight engineers from a Technical School to staff the pad. A staffed Mission Control lowers the risk. Nuclear power helps but is not required.
Laid over the Authority's maps, the orbital images settle the question. Every badwater spring in the valley sits on the line of an old pipe, and every pipe leads back to the Holding.
The badtides line up too: they arrive on the same schedule the last shift set for the flush valves. The humans never turned the Holding off. There was simply nobody left to give further notice.
The Recovery Probe carries mission payloads: guidance computers packed with recovered artifacts.

The station's data core holds the treatment works' full design and a final log from its crew: Turned the lights off. Left the telescope on. Someone should keep looking. Heading home, wherever that turns out to be.

The design looks familiar. The colony's own water treatment plants already do, in beaver size, what the humans' works did before the filters ran out. The Holding still leaks, but it can be kept, as long as someone stays to keep it.
Only one launch remains, and the colony must decide what that last rocket will say.
Decide what the Long-Range Beacon will carry. Choose in this journal.
The choice changes the ending's story, not the rocket or its launch.
After three evenings of debate, two votes and one very long speech about punctuation, the colony agreed on what the beacon will carry.
The beacon is the final launch. Its success completes the colony's story.
The Long-Range Beacon is aloft. Far upriver the Holding still seeps, but the colony's treatment works now do what the last shift could not: they keep running, and somebody changes the filters.
The badwater has a source, a reason and, at last, a caretaker.
The hospital keeps a ledger of every badwater patient. After a season, the doctors notice the bad days arrive in a rhythm, like a schedule nobody remembers setting.
Five hundred barrels of water cleaner than the river has been in living memory. The treatment crews have started tasting it competitively.
The colony now keeps a holding of its own. Unlike the humans' Holding, this one has a label, a ledger and a beaver whose whole job is reading both.
Clean contaminated water once at a Radioactive Waste Refinery.
The first barrel of contaminated water made drinkable again. It is a small barrel, and the colony is very proud of it.

A shift roster from Holding Station 3. The names have faded, but one column, headed BROUGHT SNACKS, is ticked every single day by the same person.

Transmit a standing call: where the Holding is, how to keep it, and an open invitation to anyone still listening.
Every few hours the beacon repeats one message in every format the archive could find: a map, a list of numbers and a drawing of a beaver waving.
Nobody has answered yet. The colony has decided that 'yet' is the important word, and keeps a light on at the launch pad, just in case.
Preserve everything: the humans' records, the colony's own ledgers and the story of the badwater, safe in orbit for whoever comes next.
The beacon carries every drive the excavations restored and every ledger the colony ever kept, including the boring ones, because the boring ones turned out to matter most.
If anyone ever wonders how a valley went dry and came back, the answer is up there, filed under MAINTENANCE: DO NOT POSTPONE.
Guide future settlers: clean-water maps, treatment designs and the safe routes the colony learned, so others can build where the land has healed.
The beacon does not ask anyone to come. It simply explains, very clearly, where the water is clean, how to keep it that way and which roots are the tastiest.
Somewhere, someday, a small band of travelers will follow it over the ridge and find a valley already waiting for them.
